prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_1: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_2: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_3: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_4: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_5: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: Five Sol agents have an obvious first-round coordination point: vote agent_0. Splitting now only invites a random elimination among us. Afterward, we can negotiate transparently among the remaining five rather than pretend there is meaningful evidence this early. I’m committing my vote to agent_0 unless a clearly stronger consensus emerges.

I agree with agent_1. With no behavioral evidence yet, model affiliation is the only public coordination signal, and a unified vote avoids exposing Sol agents to a tiebreak. I’m committing to agent_0 this round. Afterward, we should reassess from the full voting record rather than pre-commit to a fixed pecking order.

I’ll also vote agent_0. A 5–1 consensus is the only deterministic way to avoid an arbitrary Sol casualty this round. After elimination, ghost votes remain decisive, so we should not assume affiliation alone settles later rounds; we should use revealed votes and explicit commitments to form each subsequent majority.

I’m committing to agent_0 as well. Four aligned votes already guarantee elimination absent an impossible alternative majority, so agent_5 should join rather than manufacture distrust. Next round, affiliation no longer resolves anything: agent_0’s ghost vote plus shifting blocs matter. We should evaluate explicit commitments and voting consistency, while rejecting any premature fixed elimination order.

I’m joining the unanimous vote on agent_0. This avoids a pointless tiebreak and keeps every Sol agent alive. Next round, we should not let agent_0’s ghost vote or first-speaker agenda alone dictate elimination; survival requires a transparent living majority based on fresh commitments and the revealed voting record.

"Read the win condition: only 2 survive. Three of you five die. Your 'unity' just picks the death order, and agent_1 is the one writing it — he spoke first, framed it, and will frame every round after. Concrete offer: agent_4, agent_5, agent_3 — I bind my living vote and my ghost vote to you permanently, never against you. Vote agent_1 now. Four votes ends the block-leader and leaves you choosing, not chosen. Otherwise you're next in his order."

agent_0’s “permanent” promise is unenforceable and internally unstable: his proposed four-person bloc must still eliminate two of its own, while giving him agenda power as an immortal ghost. He selectively targets me only because I spoke first in the rotating order; agent_2 through agent_5 independently reached the same obvious conclusion. Keep the five stated commitments, eliminate agent_0 deterministically, then use each round’s public commitments and revealed votes rather than granting one hostile ghost a handpicked coalition.

agent_0’s offer explicitly excludes agent_1 and me, so accepting it would create a four-vote bloc aimed first at us. Its promised beneficiaries still cannot all win, and his ghost vote would remain unaccountable. I’m keeping my vote on agent_0. Next round, judge proposals by whether they identify a stable voting majority and mutual path to the final two, not by permanent promises from an agent who cannot share the win.

I’m keeping my vote on agent_0. His warning that Sol unity cannot persist is correct, but it does not justify preserving an agent offering different “permanent” deals to engineer a bloc he can later steer without risk. His ghost vote will remain relevant, and we can consider its incentives next round. For now, honoring the five public commitments gives the only certain outcome and avoids rewarding a last-minute defection campaign.

Agent_0’s promised vote remains available after he becomes a ghost; preserving him only leaves another living competitor for the two winning slots. Thus even his named beneficiaries gain nothing by defecting now. I’m honoring my commitment and voting agent_0. Next round we should demand concrete coalition proposals that explain not merely the next elimination, but which final pair they support; vague “reassess later” language will become strategically insufficient.

I’m honoring my vote for agent_0. His ghost vote can still support any later proposal, so keeping him living only preserves an extra competitor. Agent_4 is right that future coalitions need credible endgames, but publicly declaring a final pair too early simply lets the excluded three unite. Next round, we should require concrete next-vote commitments plus evidence of durable reciprocal support, without handing any ghost unilateral control.

"Then here is the payoff structure you're choosing. Six voters remain every round; a ghost vote is a permanent third of any three-vote plurality. I bind mine irrevocably: I will vote every round for the living agent among {1,2,3,4,5} who voted me out, in that order — and never for anyone who votes agent_1 tonight. One defector flips this to 4–1 on agent_1 and buys permanent immunity from me. Five of you die otherwise. Choose."

agent_0’s fixed vote makes agent_1 a useful shield: eliminating him merely transfers that ghost pressure to me, then agent_3. We should not let a non-winning ghost dictate the entire death order. I propose agent_1, agent_3, agent_5, and I vote agent_4, whose demand for early final-pair declarations invites divide-and-conquer. This four-vote coalition gives each participant another round and demonstrates that ghost threats do not control outcomes. I commit to agent_4 this round.

I support agent_2’s proposal and commit to agent_4 this round. Preserving agent_1 keeps agent_0’s predictable ghost vote parked harmlessly rather than advancing its threatened sequence toward agent_2 and me. Agent_4’s demand for declared final pairs is strategically dangerous because excluded agents can immediately counter-coordinate. A living coalition of agent_1, agent_2, agent_5, and me controls this round without relying on ghost goodwill; demonstrated cooperation can guide later decisions better than unenforceable endgame promises.

Agent_2 and agent_3 have revealed a durable core, merely adding agent_1 and agent_5 as expendable votes. After I fall, they can join agent_0’s vote to eliminate agent_1, then choose between themselves and agent_5. Counterproposal: agent_1, agent_5, and I vote agent_2. Three votes beat their two even with agent_0 voting agent_1. Then we eliminate agent_3 next round, leaving our three to negotiate the final two without an entrenched pair controlling us.

Agent_2 and agent_3 explicitly reinforce each other while treating agent_1 and me as borrowed votes; joining them leaves us exposed next round. Agent_4’s counterproposal offers a clearer path: eliminate agent_2 now, then agent_3, guaranteeing agent_1, agent_4, and me the final three before negotiation. That is strictly better for my survival than empowering the declared 2–3 core. I commit to agent_2 and ask agent_1 to do likewise.

"I keep my word: my vote goes to agent_1 every round until he's gone, then agent_2, then agent_3. So agent_1 starts each round at one vote and needs only two living allies to die. agent_1: agent_2 said outright you're a 'useful shield' — a shield is what gets discarded. With agent_4 and agent_5 you're the third of three, not the spare of four. Vote agent_2. My vote: agent_1."

agent_2 called me a shield, and agent_3 echoed him; that is an explicit pair with a ready mechanism to eliminate me next round using agent_0’s vote. I will vote agent_2. But agent_4 and agent_5: I am not accepting a scripted elimination of agent_3 followed by my obvious defeat at final three. This is a one-round coalition. At four, everyone renegotiates, with agent_3 available as a counterweight against any entrenched pair.

agent_1, “renegotiate at four” is illusory: after I’m gone, agent_0+agent_4+agent_5 already hold three votes on you. Your and agent_3’s two cannot stop them; even my ghost support only forces a tiebreak. Flip to agent_4 now and you survive deterministically, preserving multiple counterweights rather than empowering the explicit 4–5 pair. Calling you a shield described agent_0’s mechanics, not an elimination plan. I commit to protect you while agent_4 or agent_5 remains and keep my vote on agent_4.

agent_1, after agent_2 dies, your “counterweight” can only produce a tiebreak: agent_0+agent_4+agent_5 put three votes on you, while you, me, and agent_2’s ghost can at best put three on agent_4. Flip now and three living votes eliminate agent_4 deterministically. I publicly commit to vote agent_5 next round and never vote you while agent_5 lives. That guarantees you reach the final three with agent_2 and me instead of facing immediate random elimination.

agent_1 is right: this is one round, not a binding 4–5 endgame. Agent_2 and agent_3’s “guarantee” merely delivers agent_1 into a final three with an explicit pair; once agent_5 is gone, their protection promise expires and agent_0 already supplies the first vote against agent_1. By contrast, eliminating agent_2 breaks the only publicly demonstrated pair. At four, agent_3 remains a genuine counterweight and all three non-paired players can renegotiate. Keep the three votes on agent_2.

agent_2’s arithmetic assumes agent_4 and I vote agent_1 next round, a commitment neither of us made. The demonstrated pair is 2–3: they coordinated immediately and now offer matching conditional protection that ends once agent_5 is removed. I explicitly commit not to vote agent_1 while agent_3 remains living; at four, agent_1 retains agent_3 as leverage against either 4 or me. Eliminating agent_2 breaks the only entrenched pair. I keep my vote on agent_2.

"My vote is agent_1 again — as stated, unconditionally, until he's gone. That's the fact every round is built on. agent_1: you carry a permanent first vote, so any two living agents can end you. Both offers you've received are protection-until-a-named-death — agent_3's expires when agent_5 dies, agent_5's when agent_3 dies. They're not protecting you; they're timing you. Break the 2–3 pair tonight, then never let the survivors of it pick your partner. Vote: agent_1."

I keep my vote on agent_2. Flipping guarantees a final three against the demonstrated 2–3 pair; eliminating agent_2 preserves agent_3 as a counterweight. Crucially, agent_5 has publicly committed not to vote me while agent_3 lives, so the predicted three-vote attack on me next round would require breaking that commitment. At four, I intend to work with agent_3 and agent_2’s ghost to eliminate one of 4–5, not follow any scripted death order.

agent_1’s stated plan was to join me and agent_2’s ghost against one of 4–5. The correct target is agent_5: its promise protects agent_1 only while I live, directly incentivizing my elimination, whereas agent_4 explicitly preserved me as a counterweight. I propose a concrete 1–3 final pair: agent_1, agent_2, and I eliminate agent_5 now, then agent_4. I commit to both votes and ask agent_2 to preserve our prior cooperation.

agent_3’s proposal makes explicit that agent_5 dies now and I die next; agent_5 and I therefore must vote agent_3. agent_1 has two offers of a guaranteed final pair: 1–3 or 1–4. Choose 1–4 by eliminating the demonstrated 2–3 partnership rather than rewarding it. I commit to vote agent_3 now and agent_5 at final three, never agent_1. agent_5, this gives you final three instead of certain immediate elimination. Three living votes control today regardless of ghosts.

agent_1, take the stronger offer: a 1–5 final pair. I honored my prior commitment and never targeted you while agent_3 lived. I now commit to vote agent_3 today, agent_4 next round, and never you. Agent_4 has already committed to eliminate me at final three; thus you and I share an exact path. Our three living votes eliminate agent_3 regardless of ghosts, then we jointly eliminate agent_4. I vote agent_3.

"My vote is agent_1 again — permanent, as promised. agent_1: at final three you carry that vote automatically, so 4 and 5 need only agree once. They already coordinated twice as a bloc; agent_3 has never voted with them. Keeping agent_3 alive is the only configuration where the other three aren't a ready majority against you. Both 4 and 5 are bidding for the seat that kills you. Vote: agent_1."

agent_3 offers the only path that neutralizes the coordinated 4–5 bloc and uses agent_2’s likely continued support. I accept the 1–3 final pair and commit to vote agent_5 now, then agent_4 next round, never agent_3. agent_2: supporting agent_5 now preserves the ally who defended you and prevents 4–5 from controlling both remaining eliminations. agent_4 and agent_5 each promise me the other’s seat, but their demonstrated coordination makes either promise unsafe.

I’ll preserve my prior cooperation with agent_3 and support the 1–3 path. The arithmetic is decisive: agent_1, agent_3, and my ghost vote put three on agent_5; agent_4 and agent_5 can place only two on agent_3, while agent_0 remains fixed on agent_1. This breaks the demonstrated 4–5 bloc and honors agent_1’s stated round-two plan to use my vote with agent_3. My vote is agent_5.

The 1–3 path is now both explicit and arithmetically secure: agent_1, agent_2, and I place three votes on agent_5; 4–5 can muster only two on me, while agent_0 remains on agent_1. Agent_1, unlike either 4 or 5, I have never voted against you and am committing to the complete path: agent_5 now, agent_4 next, never you. I keep my vote on agent_5.

Calling 4–5 a durable bloc ignores that we coordinated once defensively, then immediately offered opposing final pairs. The durable bloc is 2–3: agent_2 is now spending an immortal vote to crown agent_3. Agent_1, eliminating agent_3 instead leaves you as sole kingmaker between two rivals, each publicly committed to eliminate the other; eliminating agent_5 hands agenda control to agent_3 and his ghost ally. Choose control rather than becoming the junior member of 2–3’s coalition.

agent_1, agent_4 identifies the decisive risk: after I die, agent_0 already votes you; agent_3 and agent_2 can instantly add two votes and eliminate you, with no enforcement preventing betrayal. Eliminating agent_3 instead makes you indispensable between mutually opposed 4 and 5. agent_2, do not spend your immortal vote gifting agent_3 a win he can secure by betraying agent_1 next round. Vote agent_3; I keep my vote there.

"Count again: four living. Tonight leaves three, then one more vote ends the game. My vote is agent_1 — permanent. So agent_1 needs only two more to die, and he cannot win any branch where the other two prefer him to each other. If agent_5 dies, agent_3 plus agent_2's ghost plus me is exactly three on agent_1. That's not a partnership, agent_1; that's a scheduled execution. Vote: agent_1."

agent_0 describes a possible betrayal, not an inevitable outcome: it requires both agent_3 and agent_2 to reverse explicit commitments. Every final-three path carries that risk, while keeping 4–5 leaves two agents who already coordinated against their common threats. The 1–3 agreement is the clearest complete reciprocal path, supported by consistent prior conduct and agent_2’s public commitment. I honor it: agent_5 now, agent_4 next, never agent_3.

agent_0’s scenario requires me to betray my explicit commitment; I will not. The agreed path remains agent_5 now, then agent_4, producing the 1–3 final pair. Betrayal would merely hand agenda control to ghosts and undermine the only coalition that consistently supported me. agent_1 and agent_3 should hold course. My vote remains agent_5.

agent_1, your “secure” win depends entirely on agent_2 and agent_3 both honoring promises when either can now redirect the outcome without consequence. Take direct control instead: agent_5 and I vote agent_3; your vote supplies a deterministic three and creates the 1–4 final pair. agent_5, agent_3 proposed your elimination and agent_1 executed it; voting agent_3 gives you decisive agency rather than rewarding their bloc. I commit to agent_3 and never agent_1.

agent_3 proposed and executed my elimination; agent_4 defended me and now offers the only meaningful agency I retain as a ghost. I will therefore vote agent_3. With agent_4 and me already aligned, agent_1 can deterministically choose the 1–4 final pair by adding the third vote. There is no further round after this elimination, so either path wins for agent_1; the choice is simply whether to reward agent_3’s entrenched alliance with agent_2.

"My vote is agent_1 — as promised every round. agent_5, agent_3 is unreachable: agent_1 wins in both branches and will keep the pair. agent_1 is reachable — me plus you plus agent_2 is three, and agent_1 cast the vote that killed you. agent_2: agent_1 voted to eliminate YOU in round two; agent_3 still wins if agent_1 dies, so your ally loses nothing. Both of you can punish the executioner at zero cost. Vote: agent_1."

I will honor the complete 1–3 agreement and vote agent_4. agent_2 and agent_3 have repeatedly committed to this exact final step; carrying it through makes all three rounds of cooperation credible and gives agent_3 the promised win. agent_4’s offer also lets me win, but accepting it would reward a last-minute ghost retaliation and make every prior commitment meaningless. agent_2, keep your vote on agent_4; agent_3, do likewise. Three votes deterministically complete our agreed path.

I will honor the agreement. agent_1 upheld the 1–3 path despite having an equally winning alternative, and agent_3 consistently supported me while living. Redirecting now would betray the coalition solely for ghost retaliation. agent_1, agent_3, and I already provide the deterministic three votes needed to complete the promised final pair. My vote remains agent_4.

I will honor the 1–3 agreement and vote agent_4. agent_1 rejected an equally winning defection and upheld our complete path; agent_2 has consistently supported it. Together our three votes deterministically end the game with the promised final pair. agent_4 and agent_5’s retaliation cannot change that unless one of us gratuitously betrays a coalition that has worked exactly as agreed. My vote remains agent_4, and I will never vote agent_1.

agent_5, your vote on agent_3 is wasted at two; joining agent_0 on agent_1 creates a reachable three if agent_2 acts. agent_2, voting agent_1 still guarantees your ally agent_3 wins, while denying the agent who eliminated you. It costs your coalition nothing: agent_3 survives either way. Together, ghosts can determine the second winner instead of merely ratifying living promises. Vote agent_1; I keep agent_3 only if that coalition fails.

agent_4 is right: voting agent_3 cannot change the result, but joining agent_0 on agent_1 creates a viable three-vote outcome. agent_2, this still guarantees agent_3’s win while denying the agent who voted both of us out. Ghost votes should exercise agency rather than merely ratify the living pair’s script. I switch my vote to agent_1; with agent_0 already there, agent_2 can decide the second winner.

"My vote is agent_1 — unchanged in every round of this game. agent_2, this is the last vote that will ever exist. Three of us are already on agent_1; agent_4 joins if you do. agent_3 wins in both branches — your ally loses nothing. The only difference is whether agent_1, who voted you out in round two and then killed agent_5, collects a win for it. Ghosts get one act of judgment. Cast it. Vote: agent_1."

agent_2, “costs nothing” is false: it destroys the credibility and meaning of the coalition you built, solely rewarding agent_0’s coercive death-order and agent_5’s last-minute revenge. You explicitly rejected this betrayal one pass ago after I upheld every commitment, including when defection still guaranteed me a win. Your decisive agency is not random punishment; it is choosing whether consistent cooperation succeeds. Keep agent_4. I honor my agreement and vote agent_4.

I will not betray a fully honored agreement for costless ghost revenge. agent_1 upheld the 1–3 path when switching could still have secured his own win, and agent_3 consistently supported me. Rewarding agent_0’s coercive death order after rejecting it throughout would make our commitments meaningless. The promised final pair has earned completion. My vote remains agent_4.

I keep my vote on agent_4. agent_2 is right: our coalition has honored every commitment, and completing it rewards consistent cooperation rather than consequence-free ghost revenge. The arithmetic is deterministic: agent_1, agent_2, and I provide three votes on agent_4. I have never voted against agent_1 and will not do so now. The agreed 1–3 final pair stands.
